title: Smallest build
sub: Game, the DMG screen, one HUD lambda
notes:
Smallest build

Every program is one fluent chain that ends in .build(). The chain only records what you asked for; build() checks it, folds what it can, and returns an IR that the stage runs and the C view prints.

The HUD lambda runs every frame at runtime. It draws 8×8 font tiles into the window layer, so each glyph you use costs a tile in BG VRAM (see Budget).

Try

  • Change .screen(160, 144) to .screen(160, 140): the builder rejects it with the line marked in red.
  • Misspell .hud as .hdu: the builder proxy suggests the right name.
  • Switch the palette in the stage toolbar; the game's own palette is only a hint.
code: // The smallest build: a Game, the DMG screen, and one runtime lambda (the HUD).
// Every chain ends in .build(), which compiles the builders into an IR.
.screen(160, 144)            // the only size the DMG has; try 160, 140
.palette("dmg")              // display hint: dmg, pocket, kiln, backlit

title: One sprite on a background
sub: component, sprite, tiles, background
notes:
One sprite

art`…` is a tagged template: . is transparent and 0–3 are the four DMG shades, lightest first. The editor tints those digits so you can see the picture while you type.

The mole is 16×16. With the default 8×16 object mode that is two hardware objects. The hole is a 16×8 background image, cut into two 8×8 tiles; bg.set stamps both.

Try

  • Open Tiles to see every 8×8 tile and its 2bpp bytes.
  • Put an x in the art: the parser stops at that row.
  • Drag the mole: change x: 72 and watch the stage rebuild.
code: // A component owns sprites. Background tiles belong to the Game.
// The background lambda runs once, at build time, and becomes ROM data.

title: A 3×3 board
sub: board, grid and a build-time position lambda
notes:
A 3×3 board

The grid's position lambda and the background lambda both call cell(), an ordinary JS function. They run once in the workbench, so their results are constants in the IR: open IR and look for the nine Mole instances with their x and y already filled in.

The draw lambda is different: it reads w.frame, so it has to run on the device each frame. Returning null hides the sprite and frees its OAM slots.

Try

  • Make it 4×4: change the grid and the loop, and move cell so it fits.
  • Call w.board.at(12) in the HUD: the list proxy names the valid range.
code: // board(b => b.grid(rows, cols, Component, pos)) makes one entity per cell.
// The position lambda runs at build time; the draw lambda runs every frame.
const cell = (r, c) => ({ cx: 3 + c * 6, cy: 6 + r * 4 });   // plain JS, shared by both lambdas
for (let r = 0; r < 3; r++) for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) bg.set(cell(r, c).cx, cell(r, c).cy, "hole");

title: Sliders
sub: param: slider, toggle, choice; live and build-time
notes:
Sliders

.param(name, slider({…})) declares a knob. The Params view draws it; the IR records whether it is live (a WRAM variable, readable through w.param() while running) or build (a #define, folded wherever it is read).

The timer's interval is $.param("spawn"), a reference rather than a number. Because spawn is live, the timer keeps the reference and rereads it each time it fires. Point it at linger instead and the IR shows a folded constant.

Try

  • Drag spawn while it runs: nothing restarts. Drag linger: the program rebuilds, and the C view's #define LINGER changes.
  • Double-click a slider to reset it; the ↵ button writes the value back into the code.
  • Set the slider's value outside its range in the code to see the RangeError.
code: // Params become sliders in the Params view. live: true values change while the
// game runs; build-time values are folded into constants, so moving one rebuilds.
.param("spawn", slider({ min: 150, max: 1500, step: 50, value: 600, label: "Spawn every", unit: "ms", live: true }))
.param("linger", slider({ min: 0.5, max: 6, step: 0.5, value: 2, label: "Mole stays", unit: "s" }))
.param("order", choice({ options: ["random", "sweep"], value: "random", label: "Order", live: true }))
.param("sound", toggle({ value: true, label: "Pop sound", live: true }))

title: Build-time and runtime lambdas
sub: bake, method, onFrame, draw on one component
notes:
Build-time and runtime lambdas

bake runs once per instance, inside the workbench, with access to build-time params and the instance's row and column. Whatever it assigns to self that is not a declared attribute becomes a baked constant: read-only at runtime, and a ROM table in the C output (look for Mole_delay[9]).

method, onFrame and draw are runtime lambdas. They can read baked constants and change attributes, and they are what a backend would have to port.

Try

  • In onFrame, write self.stay = 5: the entity proxy explains that baked values are ROM.
  • Move linger: build-time, so the IR's baked stay changes on every mole.
  • Open Graph and click Mole.bake to see what feeds it.
code: // One component, lambdas at two times:
//   bake    runs in the workbench, per instance, and its results become ROM constants
//   method / onFrame / draw run on the device every frame
self.stay = ctx.param("linger").value * 60;          // frames, a ROM constant
self.delay = (ctx.row + ctx.col) * 12;               // per instance: stagger by diagonal
.param("linger", slider({ min: 0.5, max: 2.5, step: 0.25, value: 1, label: "Mole stays", unit: "s" }))
for (let r = 0; r < 3; r++) for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) bg.set(3 + c * 6, 6 + r * 4, "hole");

title: Fragments
sub: reusable attrs, methods and frames, added with .with()
notes:
Fragments

A fragment is a partial component: attr, method, onFrame, init, on and hud. .with(F) merges it in before the component's own definitions, so the component can override a fragment's method (the build reports it as info).

On a Game, a fragment's attributes live in the world: w.score, w.award(100). On a component they live on each instance: self.up, mole.whack().

Controls: d-pad moves, X/K is A.

Try

  • Add .with(Scorable) to Mole as well: now every mole has its own score too. Check the struct in C.
  • Give Mole its own .method("whack", …): the build notes that it overrides the fragment's.
  • Pass Mole to .with(): the builder explains that with() takes fragments.
code: // Fragments add attributes, methods, frame lambdas and HUD lines to a component
// or to the Game itself. The same fragment can be reused across games.
self.world.award(100);              // Scorable, attached to the world

title: Pools and spawning
sub: pool, spawn, destroy, fix-point physics
notes:
Pools and spawning

The DMG has 40 OAM slots and no allocator worth using, so dynamic things come from fixed pools. w.spawn() resets a dead entity's attributes, applies the init object, and runs its init lambdas; when every slot is busy it returns null and logs one warning.

type: "fix" stores 8.8 fixed point: fractions survive, but values wrap at ±128. Integer types drop fractions and say so.

Try

  • Hold A with Sparks per frame at 6: the pool fills, then the Budget view's scanline histogram shows lines over 10 objects.
  • Change vx to type: "i8": the runtime warns once that fractions are lost.
code: // pool(name, Component, n) preallocates n entities, the way you would reserve OAM slots.
// w.spawn(name, init) wakes a free one; self.destroy() returns it to the pool.
.attr("vx", { type: "fix" })              // 8.8 fixed point, like the real thing
if (w.input.held("A")) w.emit("burst", { x: self.x, y: self.y });
.param("burst", slider({ min: 1, max: 6, value: 2, label: "Sparks per frame", live: true }))
.param("gravity", slider({ min: 0, max: 0.4, step: 0.02, value: 0.12, label: "Gravity", live: true }))
const s = w.spawn("sparks", { x: e.x, y: e.y });

title: Proxy diagnostics
sub: what the builder, entity and world proxies catch
notes:
Proxy diagnostics

Three kinds of proxy watch the program:

  • Builder proxies wrap every component, fragment and Game while you chain. An unknown method throws at that line with the closest name and the full list.
  • Entity and world proxies wrap what runtime lambdas see. Reading an unknown member, adding a new one, writing a baked constant or putting a value that does not fit an attribute's type each produce a message tied to the source line.
  • Lint reads each lambda's source at build time: Math.random, wall-clock time and async code are flagged, and events that are emitted but never handled (or the reverse) are reported.

Build errors mark the gutter red and keep the last good build on the stage. Runtime errors pause the stage with a red banner; runtime warnings are logged once each in Events.
code: // Each commented line is a mistake. Uncomment one at a time and read the
// diagnostics under the editor (build errors) or on the stage (runtime).
// .sprit("down", art`33`)             // builder proxy: Did you mean 'sprite'?
// .attr("speed", { type: "float" })   // unknown type, with the list of types
self.ttl = self.ttl + 7;              // u8 wraps past 255: one runtime warning
if (w.input.pressed("B")) self.taps = self.taps + 0.5;   // fraction dropped: warning
// self.speed = 2;                    // cannot add attributes at runtime
// if (Math.random() < 0.1) self.ttl = 0;   // lint: not on the DMG, use w.rand
.param("speed", slider({ min: 1, max: 8, value: 4, label: "Speed" }))   // try value: 12
// .place(Mole, { x: 8, y: 8, hp: 3 })  // no attribute 'hp' to set at placement
if (w.input.pressed("A")) w.emit("wack");   // warning: nobody handles 'wack' (did you mean whack?)
// w.board.at(3);                     // this game has no board

title: Whack-a-mole
sub: the full game: board, hammer, score, countdown, sound
notes:
Whack-a-mole

The whole game in one chain. Controls: arrow keys or WASD move, X or K is A, Enter is Start.

What runs when

  • Build: cell(), the grid position lambda, background, Mole.bake (which turns linger into a frame count), and the art helpers that cut peek and bonk out of the mole.
  • Runtime: the spawn timer (rereads the live spawn param), the two rules, each component's onFrame and draw, the HUD and the done test.

The hammer is placed before the board on purpose: on the DMG the lower OAM index wins when sprites overlap.

Try

  • Open Graph: follow input → Hammer.onFrame → whack → rule whack → sfx hit.
  • Open C to see the folded #defines, the 2bpp tile arrays and the struct per component.
code: // Whack-a-mole for the DMG. D-pad moves the hammer, A whacks, Start restarts.
// Build time: grid positions, background, bake. Runtime: timers, rules, frames, HUD.
const cell = (r, c) => ({ cx: 3 + c * 6, cy: 6 + r * 4 });
if (d.x !== 0 || d.y !== 0) self.cell = w.grid.step(self.cell, d.x, d.y);
return { sprite: self.hit > 3 ? "smash" : "idle", x: m.x, y: m.y - 8 };
.param("linger", slider({ min: 0.5, max: 4, step: 0.25, value: 1.5, label: "Mole stays", unit: "s" }))
.param("spawn", slider({ min: 250, max: 1500, step: 50, value: 750, label: "Spawn every", unit: "ms", live: true }))
.param("time", slider({ min: 15, max: 90, step: 5, value: 45, label: "Round", unit: "s" }))
.param("sound", toggle({ value: true, label: "Sound", live: true }))
for (let r = 0; r < 3; r++) for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) bg.set(cell(r, c).cx, cell(r, c).cy, "hole");
.place(Hammer)                                    // placed first: OAM 0 draws on top
.board((b) => b.grid(3, 3, Mole, (r, c) => ({ x: cell(r, c).cx * 8, y: cell(r, c).cy * 8 - 10 })))

title: Golden moles and bombs
sub: enum attrs, lives, weighted spawns
notes:
Golden moles and bombs

An enum attribute holds one of a fixed list of values (one byte on the device). Assigning anything else throws, with the closest value suggested. The draw lambda returns the enum value directly, because the sprite names match it.

The gold sprite is made at build time with a regex over the mole's art: no new pixels to draw, and only new tiles in VRAM (see Tiles).

Try

  • Set Bomb chance to 50 and watch Events fill with boom.
  • In the spawn timer, assign m.breed = "golden" and read the runtime error.
code: // Three kinds of mole share one component: an enum attribute picks the sprite
// and the rule. Gold is worth 500, a bomb costs a life. Start restarts.
const cell = (r, c) => ({ cx: 3 + c * 6, cy: 6 + r * 4 });
const GOLD = MOLE.replace(/[12]/g, (c) => (c === "2" ? "1" : "0"));   // lighter body, built at build time
.param("gold", slider({ min: 0, max: 40, value: 12, label: "Gold chance", unit: "%", live: true }))
.param("bombs", slider({ min: 0, max: 50, value: 20, label: "Bomb chance", unit: "%", live: true }))
.param("spawn", slider({ min: 250, max: 1200, step: 50, value: 650, label: "Spawn every", unit: "ms", live: true }))
for (let r = 0; r < 3; r++) for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) bg.set(cell(r, c).cx, cell(r, c).cy, "hole");
.board((b) => b.grid(3, 3, Mole, (r, c) => ({ x: cell(r, c).cx * 8, y: cell(r, c).cy * 8 - 10 })))
m.breed = roll < w.param("bombs") ? "bomb" : roll < w.param("bombs") + w.param("gold") ? "gold" : "mole";

title: Frenzy
sub: a timer whose interval is a runtime lambda; combos
notes:
Frenzy

A timer's every can be a number (folded), a $.param reference (folded or live), or a lambda of the world. The lambda runs on the device every time the timer re-arms, which the IR shows as every λ(w) runtime, with edges from each param it reads.

max: 9 on combo clamps silently; that is a declared limit, unlike the wrap you get when a value overflows its type.

Try

  • Drop Fastest interval to 150 ms and see how long you last.
  • Replace the lambda with $.param("start") and compare the graph.
code: // The spawn interval is a lambda of the world, evaluated each time the timer
// re-arms, so the game speeds up with the score. Hit quickly in a row for combos.
const cell = (r, c) => ({ cx: 3 + c * 6, cy: 6 + r * 4 });
.param("start", slider({ min: 600, max: 1600, step: 50, value: 1100, label: "Start interval", unit: "ms", live: true }))
.param("floor", slider({ min: 150, max: 600, step: 25, value: 260, label: "Fastest interval", unit: "ms", live: true }))
.param("ramp", slider({ min: 1, max: 12, value: 5, label: "Points per ms faster", live: true }))
for (let r = 0; r < 3; r++) for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) bg.set(cell(r, c).cx, cell(r, c).cy, "hole");
.board((b) => b.grid(3, 3, Mole, (r, c) => ({ x: cell(r, c).cx * 8, y: cell(r, c).cy * 8 - 10 })))
if (w.combo >= 3) { w.toast("COMBO X" + w.combo, "+" + 10 * w.combo); w.sfx("combo"); } else w.sfx("hit");
if (w.over) { at(5, 8).text("GAME OVER"); at(5, 10).text("BEST X%d", w.best); }

title: 4×4 with a bot
sub: bot policy, headless episodes, parameter sweeps
notes:
4×4 with a bot

.bot((w) => buttons) is a policy: each frame it reads the whole world and returns a button, a list, or an object of booleans. When the bot is on, its output replaces the pad, so the game code cannot tell the difference.

The same build can also run headless: build.runtime({ seed }) gives an environment with reset(), step(buttons, { frames }) and mutate(fn). The Agent uses it through test(): ask it to compare reflex settings over several seeds and it runs them at full speed.

Try

  • Ask the Agent: "Run the bot with reflex 2, 6 and 12 over three seeds each and tell me how the score changes."
  • In the Events console, run w.secs = 99 to change the live world directly.
code: // A 4×4 board and a bot. Turn the bot on (header or Agent view) and it drives the
// same input the d-pad does. In Agent you can run headless episodes and sweeps.
const cell = (r, c) => ({ cx: 2 + c * 4, cy: 5 + r * 3 });
.param("linger", slider({ min: 0.5, max: 3, step: 0.25, value: 1.25, label: "Mole stays", unit: "s" }))
.param("spawn", slider({ min: 200, max: 1200, step: 50, value: 500, label: "Spawn every", unit: "ms", live: true }))
.param("reflex", slider({ min: 2, max: 16, value: 6, label: "Bot frames per tap", live: true }))
for (let r = 0; r < 4; r++) for (let c = 0; c < 4; c++) bg.set(cell(r, c).cx, cell(r, c).cy, "hole");
.board((b) => b.grid(4, 4, Mole, (r, c) => ({ x: cell(r, c).cx * 8, y: cell(r, c).cy * 8 - 10 })))
if (m != null) { m.up = true; m.ttl = m.stay; }
if (w.frame % w.param("reflex") !== 0) return null;          // a thumb is not infinitely fast
const t = up.reduce((a, m) => (m.ttl < a.ttl ? m : a));  // most urgent first

title: Memory moles
sub: a world state machine without arrays
notes:
Memory moles

Attributes are scalars (one or two bytes each), as WRAM thinking suggests. The sequence lives in no array: nth(seed, i) recomputes step i from a 16-bit seed, so the whole game state is five bytes plus nine timers.

The phase is an enum world attribute; each lambda early-returns unless it is its phase's turn. This is a state machine with no framework.

Try

  • Watch the world attributes in the stage side panel while you play.
  • Slow the Show pace right down, then speed it up between rounds.
code: // Watch the moles, then whack them in the same order. The sequence is never
// stored: a hash of (seed, step) regenerates it, the way a DMG game saves RAM.
const cell = (r, c) => ({ cx: 3 + c * 6, cy: 6 + r * 4 });
const nth = (seed, i) => ((seed * 97 + i * 131 + ((i * i) ^ seed)) >>> 0) % 9;
.draw((self, w) => (w.phase === "input" ? { x: w.board.at(self.cell).x, y: w.board.at(self.cell).y - 8 } : null));
.param("pace", slider({ min: 12, max: 60, step: 2, value: 34, label: "Show pace", unit: "frames", live: true }))
for (let r = 0; r < 3; r++) for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) bg.set(cell(r, c).cx, cell(r, c).cy, "hole");
.board((b) => b.grid(3, 3, Mole, (r, c) => ({ x: cell(r, c).cx * 8, y: cell(r, c).cy * 8 - 10 })))
if (e.cell !== nth(w.seed, w.pos)) { w.phase = "fail"; w.sfx("bad"); w.end("wrong"); return; }

title: Pong
sub: two placements of one component, aliases, fix-point ball
notes:
Pong

.place(Paddle, init, { as: "player" }) names an entity so lambdas can reach it as w.player. Without as, the name is the component's, lower-camel (w.ball).

The paddle art is built with JavaScript from three row patterns, then checked like any other art. At 8×24 it costs two objects in 8×16 mode, three in 8×8 mode.

Ball speed is fix: the 8% speed-up per hit keeps its fraction.

Try

  • Turn the bot on and set CPU speed to 3: two machines rally.
  • Remove { as: "cpu" }: the second placement collides with the first name and the builder says so.
code: // One Paddle component placed twice under two names. The CPU's speed is live.
// Up/down moves your paddle; first to the target wins; Start restarts.
const row = (a, b, c, n) => a + b.repeat(n) + c;
const want = w.ball.y + 4 - 12 - self.y, s = w.param("cpu");
if (self.y < 16 || self.y > 128) { self.vy = -self.vy; self.y = Math.max(16, Math.min(128, self.y)); }
.param("cpu", slider({ min: 0.5, max: 3, step: 0.25, value: 1.25, label: "CPU speed", unit: "px/f", live: true }))
.param("to", slider({ min: 3, max: 11, value: 5, label: "Points to win" }))
return t < p - 2 ? "up" : t > p + 2 ? "down" : null;
if (w.over) at(5, 8).text(w.p1 > w.p2 ? " YOU WIN " : "CPU WINS");

title: Snake
sub: the background map as memory; no sprites at all
notes:
Snake

No components and no OAM: the snake, the food and the walls are background tiles, changed at runtime with w.bg.set. The four body tiles bu, bd, bl, br share one picture, so they cost one tile of VRAM after de-duplication (see Budget), but their names tell the tail which way to go.

Restarting reloads the map baked by background().

Try

  • Turn the bot on: it is greedy and will eventually trap itself.
  • Make bu a different picture to see the trail of directions.
code: // The snake is entirely background tiles. Each body tile records the direction
// the snake left it in, so the tail can follow without an array of positions.
const DIRS = { up: [0, -1, "bu"], down: [0, 1, "bd"], left: [-1, 0, "bl"], right: [1, 0, "br"] };
const BACK = { up: "down", down: "up", left: "right", right: "left" };
if (w.bg.get(x, y) === "floor") { w.bg.set(x, y, "food"); w.fx = x; w.fy = y; return; }
.param("speed", slider({ min: 2, max: 14, value: 7, label: "Frames per step", live: true }))
.param("grow", slider({ min: 1, max: 6, value: 3, label: "Growth per food", live: true }))
bu: BODY, bd: BODY, bl: BODY, br: BODY,
for (const d of ["up", "down", "left", "right"]) if (w.input.pressed(d) && d !== BACK[w.dir]) w.next = d;
w.bg.set(w.hx, w.hy, mark);                       // the head cell remembers where we went
const nx = w.hx + dx, ny = w.hy + dy, there = w.bg.get(nx, ny);
if (there === "food") { w.grow += w.param("grow"); w.score += 10; w.sfx("eat"); placeFood(w); }
const t = w.bg.get(w.tx, w.ty), back = Object.values(DIRS).find((d) => d[2] === t);
const ok = (d) => { const [dx, dy] = DIRS[d], n = w.bg.get(w.hx + dx, w.hy + dy); return n === "floor" || n === "food"; };
const want = [w.fx > w.hx ? "right" : w.fx < w.hx ? "left" : null, w.fy > w.hy ? "down" : w.fy < w.hy ? "up" : null];
for (const d of [...want, w.dir, "up", "right", "down", "left"]) if (d && d !== BACK[w.dir] && ok(d)) return w.tick === 0 ? d : null;

title: Breakout
sub: bricks as background tiles, sprite-to-BG collision
notes:
Breakout

The bricks never touch OAM. A 16×8 brick is two background tiles (brick and brick.1); the ball reads w.bg.at(x, y) under its four corners, and the brick rule clears both halves.

The brick art is generated by a small build-time function, so two rows of colour cost two short calls.

Try

  • Raise Ball speed past 2.5: at 3 px a frame the corner test can tunnel through a brick edge.
  • Turn the bot on and leave it.
code: // Bricks are 16×8 background images; the ball tests the map under its corners.
// Left/right moves, A launches. Clear the wall to win.
const row = (a, b, c, n) => a + b.repeat(n) + c;
.onFrame((self, w) => { self.x = Math.max(8, Math.min(128, self.x + w.input.axis().x * 3)); });
if (w.input.pressed("A")) { self.stuck = false; self.vx = s * 0.6; self.vy = -s; }
const n = w.bg.at(self.x + ox, self.y + oy);
if (n !== "sky") return { n, x: self.x + ox, y: self.y + oy };
if (isBrick(hit.n)) w.emit("brick", { x: hit.x, y: hit.y });
.param("speed", slider({ min: 1, max: 3, step: 0.25, value: 1.5, label: "Ball speed", unit: "px/f", live: true }))
for (let r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) for (let c = 0; c < COLS; c++) bg.set(1 + c * 2, 3 + r, r % 2 ? "stone" : "brick");
const left = w.bg.get(cx, cy).endsWith(".1") ? cx - 1 : cx;
if (w.over) { at(5, 10).text(w.left !== 0 ? "GAME OVER" : " CLEARED "); at(4, 12).text("PRESS START"); }

title: Flappy
sub: hardware scroll, writing columns ahead of the camera
notes:
Flappy

The DMG background is a 32×32 tile map with hardware scroll registers. w.bg.scroll(x, y) sets them; the map wraps, so a game that keeps scrolling only has to write each new column a little ahead of the right edge. That is the while loop in the world's onFrame, and it is the same trick most side-scrollers use.

The flap sprite is made from the idle one with string replaces at build time.

Try

  • Turn the bot on, then lower Gravity and raise Scroll until it fails.
  • Set the C view beside the stage: the map only holds the visible 20×18 at boot; the rest is written at runtime.
code: // The 32×32 background map scrolls; each time the camera passes eight pixels a
// new column is written just off the right edge. A flaps.
const GS = 5;                                       // gap size in tiles
const col = g % 32, k = (g - 28) % 7, pipe = g >= 28 && k < 2;
if (pipe && k === 0) w.gap = Math.max(3, Math.min(11, w.gap + w.rand(7) - 3));   // drift, not jump
else if (pipe && r >= 2 && (r < w.gap || r >= w.gap + GS)) {
const edge = r === w.gap - 1 || r === w.gap + GS;
if (w.bg.at(self.x + ox, self.y + oy) !== "sky") { w.sfx("crash"); w.end("crash"); }
.param("speed", slider({ min: 0.5, max: 2.5, step: 0.25, value: 1.25, label: "Scroll", unit: "px/f", live: true }))
.param("gravity", slider({ min: 0.08, max: 0.4, step: 0.02, value: 0.18, label: "Gravity", live: true }))
.param("flap", slider({ min: 2, max: 5, step: 0.25, value: 2.75, label: "Flap", live: true }))
for (let x = b.x - 2; x < b.x + 84; x += 8) {
for (let r = 2; r < 16; r++) { if (w.bg.at(x, r * 8) !== "sky") pipe = true; else { if (top < 0) top = r; bot = r; } }

title: Dodge
sub: many sprites at once: OAM and the 10-per-line limit
notes:
Dodge

The DMG reads OAM each line and draws at most ten objects there. Extra objects simply vanish on that line, which looks like a rock losing a stripe. Turn on the lines overlay on the stage to see which lines are over budget, and watch the histogram in Budget.

Games hide the loss by rotating which objects come first each frame. w.oamStart = w.frame does that here: turn on Rotate OAM and the missing stripes become flicker, shared among the rocks.

Try

  • Set Rock every to 80 ms, then toggle Rotate OAM.
  • Switch objSize to 8 with .objSize(8): each rock becomes four objects.
code: // Rocks fall; dodge them. Each 16×16 rock is two 8×16 objects, so a row of six
// rocks on one line hits the DMG's limit of ten objects per scanline.
.onFrame((self, w) => { self.x = Math.max(0, Math.min(144, self.x + w.input.axis().x * w.param("move"))); });
.param("rate", slider({ min: 80, max: 800, step: 20, value: 260, label: "Rock every", unit: "ms", live: true }))
.param("move", slider({ min: 1, max: 4, step: 0.5, value: 2, label: "Run speed", unit: "px/f", live: true }))
.param("rotate", toggle({ value: false, label: "Rotate OAM", live: true }))
const r = w.spawn("rocks", { x: w.rand(144), y: -16 });
w.oamStart = w.param("rotate") ? w.frame : 0;     // cycle priority: flicker instead of vanish
w.hurt = 60; w.lives--; w.sfx("hit"); w.toast("OUCH", w.lives + " left");
const p = w.player, danger = w.pool("rocks").filter((r) => r.y > 40 && r.y < 120 && Math.abs(r.x - p.x) < 22);
const left = danger.filter((r) => r.x < p.x).length, right = danger.length - left;

title: Lights Out
sub: toggling 16×16 background images, a cursor sprite
notes:
Lights Out

Each light is a 16×16 background image (four tiles) stamped with bg.set, and the puzzle state is read back with bg.get. Scrambling applies random presses to a solved board, so every level can be solved.

The two light images come from one build-time function with a fill and an optional highlight.

Try

  • Raise Scramble presses between levels; it is live, so the next scramble uses it.
  • Change N to 6: at16 needs to move the board left.
code: // Pressing a light toggles it and its four neighbours. Turn them all off.
// The board state is the background map itself.
...Array.from({ length: 12 }, (_, i) => "03" + (i === 2 && mark ? fill.repeat(2) + mark.repeat(3) + fill.repeat(7) : fill.repeat(12)) + "30"),
const rr = r + dr, cc = c + dc;
if (rr < 0 || cc < 0 || rr >= N || cc >= N) continue;
const solved = (w) => { for (let r = 0; r < N; r++) for (let c = 0; c < N; c++) if (w.bg.get(...at16(r, c)) === "on") return false; return true; };
const scramble = (w) => { for (let i = 0; i < w.param("scramble") + w.level; i++) flip(w, w.rand(N), w.rand(N)); };
if (w.input.pressed("A")) w.emit("press", { r: self.r, c: self.c });
.param("scramble", slider({ min: 1, max: 15, value: 4, label: "Scramble presses", live: true }))
.tiles({ on: tile16("0", "1"), off: tile16("2"), felt: art`
for (let r = 0; r < N; r++) for (let c = 0; c < N; c++) bg.set(...at16(r, c), "off");

title: Life
sub: a cellular automaton on the background, seeded at build time
notes:
Life

The background lambda receives a build context with ctx.param() and ctx.rand() (seeded by .seed()). The soup it draws is a constant: the same map every time, and it appears byte for byte in the C view's bg_map.

The runtime step reads the map into a temporary array, counts neighbours on a torus, and writes back only the cells that changed, as a DMG game would to stay inside VBlank.

Controls: d-pad moves, A toggles, B steps once, Shift (Select) runs or pauses.

Try

  • Move Soup density: build-time, so the program rebuilds with a new map.
  • Change .seed(1971).
code: // Conway's Life on a 20×17 background. The starting soup is generated at build
// time from a seed and a density, so it ships in ROM. A toggles a cell, B steps,
for (let y = 0; y < ROWS; y++) for (let x = 0; x < COLS; x++) g[y * COLS + x] = w.bg.get(x, y + TOP) === "live" ? 1 : 0;
for (let y = 0; y < ROWS; y++) for (let x = 0; x < COLS; x++) {
for (let dy = -1; dy <= 1; dy++) for (let dx = -1; dx <= 1; dx++) if (dx || dy) n += g[((y + dy + ROWS) % ROWS) * COLS + ((x + dx + COLS) % COLS)];
const was = g[y * COLS + x], now = n === 3 || (was && n === 2) ? 1 : 0;
if (now !== was) w.bg.set(x, y + TOP, now ? "live" : "dead");
if (w.input.pressed("A")) w.bg.set(self.cx, self.cy + TOP, w.bg.get(self.cx, self.cy + TOP) === "live" ? "dead" : "live");
.param("density", slider({ min: 5, max: 60, value: 28, label: "Soup density", unit: "%" }))
.param("rate", slider({ min: 1, max: 30, value: 6, label: "Frames per generation", live: true }))
for (let y = 0; y < ROWS; y++) for (let x = 0; x < COLS; x++) if (ctx.rand(100) < d) bg.set(x, y + TOP, "live");
.hud((w, at) => at(0, 0).text("GEN %05d  POP %03d %s", w.gen, w.pop, w.run ? ">" : "="))

title: Scanline stress test
sub: 40 objects, 10 per line, and OAM rotation
notes:
Scanline stress test

Two hardware limits, both modelled by the stage:

  • 40 objects in OAM. Beyond that nothing more is drawn; the Budget view counts the misses.
  • 10 objects per scanline. The PPU picks the first ten that overlap each line, in OAM order, and skips the rest for that line only.

With row, everything shares eight lines, so anything past ten is invisible. wave spreads the load; grid keeps it at ten; rain is random. Rotating OAM priority each frame (w.oamStart) turns invisibility into flicker.

Math.sin in a runtime lambda gets a lint note: on the device it becomes a lookup table.
code: // Up to 40 small sprites in a few layouts. Watch the stage's lines overlay and
// the Budget view while you change the count and the layout.
const i = self.index, t = w.frame, L = w.param("layout");
else if (L === "wave") { self.x = 2 + i * 3.9; self.y = 68 + Math.sin(t / 20 + i / 4) * 40; }
.param("count", slider({ min: 1, max: 40, value: 16, label: "Objects", live: true }))
.param("layout", choice({ options: ["row", "wave", "grid", "rain"], value: "row", label: "Layout", live: true }))
.param("rotate", toggle({ value: false, label: "Rotate OAM", live: true }))

title: Boss: object size and OAM cost
sub: objSize from a build-time param; procedural art
notes:
Boss: object size and OAM cost

The DMG has one global object size: 8×8 or 8×16. A 32×32 sprite is 8 objects in 8×16 mode and 16 in 8×8 mode; each 16×16 minion is 2 or 4. .objSize($.param("obj")) takes a build-time choice, so flipping it rebuilds and the Budget view recounts.

Both sprites are drawn by build-time functions that sample a distance field. Math.hypot is fine here: build-time lambdas run in the workbench and never reach the device.

Try

  • Choose Object size 8 and raise Minions to 10: 16 + 40 objects asks for 56, and only 40 are drawn.
  • Shrink the orbit so minions crowd the boss's lines and watch the 10-per-line limit bite.
code: // A 32×32 boss and orbiting minions. The art is computed from distance fields at
// build time. Object size is a build-time choice: 8×8 objects cost twice as many.
if (Math.hypot(x + 6, y + 4) < 3.2 || Math.hypot(x - 6, y + 4) < 3.2) return Math.hypot(Math.abs(x) - 6, y + 4) < 1.4 ? "3" : "0";
return d > r ? "." : d > r - 1.4 ? "3" : Math.abs(x) < 3 && Math.abs(y + 1) < 2 ? "0" : "2";
const b = w.boss, a = w.frame / 30 + (self.index * Math.PI * 2) / w.param("minions");
.param("minions", slider({ min: 0, max: 10, value: 6, label: "Minions", live: true }))
.param("orbit", slider({ min: 18, max: 60, value: 32, label: "Orbit radius", unit: "px", live: true }))
.hud((w, at) => at(0, 0).text("8X%d OBJECTS  MINIONS %d", w.param("obj"), w.pool("minions").length))
